name: Liam Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we do not sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Liam Tanaka, 43, working as a junior construction hand on carpentry and general site jobs. I live with my partner and our two school-age children; the mortgage is the large fixed bill, and I keep a folding ruler in my back pocket all day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a usual shift involve for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I unload boards, carry frames into the building, mark lengths and help the carpenter line things up. I am still learning, so I ask before making a cut; I like the quiet first hour before deliveries make the site noisy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say an accurate delivery list saves us a trip back to the yard. I would still check the boards against the frame before cutting, because the screen does not see what is crooked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do more carrying and fitting than computer work, so this small change would not replace most of my shift. A cancelled site day is a bigger worry because we have very little saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the site shifts and check with the supervisor before the end of each week about the next one. If work slows, I would wait to replace my work boots until the sole really needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small AI change does not make me want to leave construction. I still feel on edge about the mortgage whenever the schedule has a blank day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the delivery would you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the length and condition of the boards before carrying them upstairs. One damaged piece can hold up the frame while we wait for another delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do now when a shift disappears from the schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I call the supervisor and ask if another crew needs help that day. If there is nothing, my partner and I move a non-urgent purchase to the next pay week.

fieldNote: He expects modest direct change to his **physical tasks** on site.

steps.text: Keep taking offered site shifts and ask about next week before Friday
Delay replacing work boots until the soles need it during a slow spell

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can use software to make delivery plans, but the crew still needs to check what arrives. I would tell people to count the waste and delays as well as the minutes saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI may take over the notes and ordering questions I sometimes help with. I use a chat tool now and then, but I do not know if I could learn the company’s planning screen quickly enough to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor to show me the delivery-planning screen on one real order. I would use the chat tool to review the terms afterward, then keep doing the lifting and fitting I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am willing to try after I have seen the tool work on a job like mine. I would feel uneasy if everyone expected me to learn it alone while still hitting the same daily target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look at to decide whether the screen is helping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the quantities it lists with what the carpenter actually uses. If we still have missing pieces or a pile left over, the quicker plan has not solved the whole problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you comfortable using a new planning screen on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want one person available for questions the first few times I use it. Once I have seen the steps repeated on two or three orders, I can try it without asking every minute.

Use AI to review its terms, then keep doing my **lifting and fitting** work.

S1.quote: If we still have missing pieces or a pile left over, the quicker plan has not solved the whole problem.
fieldNote: He weighs **material waste and delays**, not just speed, when judging the tool.
He is open to a **proven screen** but wants early help using it.

steps.text: Learn the delivery-planning screen with the supervisor on a real order
Keep taking current lifting and fitting shifts while learning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office work could change by 2028, while robots for carrying and fitting come later. I would not tell my crew that those extra years mean the same site work is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could do the delivery plan and the measurement notes I sometimes help prepare. I would need to rely more on practical work, but that work could also be affected when robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028, I would ask the carpenter to teach me to hang a door and check the frame. In 2029, I would take the shifts I can get and only save from a week when the main bills are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is short when I am still making basic mistakes. I would try to improve, but I cannot say that a better door fit will keep our income steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might happen at home if your hours dropped in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would put off a family purchase and check the mortgage date before anything else. I would tell the children the plan changed because work was short, not because they had asked for too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years before robots give you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They give me some time to learn practical work while sites still hire, if they do. I would ask around about shifts, but I would not count on a vacancy being there.

say: I would say **office tasks change first**, before robots reach carrying and fitting work.
I would not call **extra years a guarantee** of the same site work.
think: I think AI could do **delivery plans** and the measurement notes I sometimes help prepare.
I may rely more on practical work, but **robots could affect it** around 2031.
do: Ask the carpenter to teach me **hanging a door** before 2028.
Save a little in 2029 only after the **main bills** are covered.
Take available **paid shifts** on site during 2029.
feel: **Two years is short** when I am still making basic mistakes.
I cannot say better work will keep **our income steady**.
S2.quote: I cannot say that a better door fit will keep our income steady.
fieldNote: He sees the 2028 loss of **planning work** and the later risk to physical tasks.
His **2029 savings plan** depends on covering bills and finding shifts.

steps.text: Learn hanging doors and checking frames with the carpenter before 2028
In 2029, save a little only after the main bills are covered
Take available paid site shifts during 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives someone like me time to get better at more than carrying boards. I would also say that nobody can promise the work will be waiting once the tools change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031, AI could handle much of the scheduling and measurement paperwork I occasionally help with. Robots follow in 2034, so even the physical part has a date attached; I cannot call carpentry a safe plan forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to practise fitting door frames and trimming boards over the next few years. In 2032, I would ask local builders what work they really need before paying for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me learn in steps instead of making a rushed move this month. It still makes me anxious because I have little savings if the training takes time to lead anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which skill would you ask to practise first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with measuring and fitting a door frame, because the gap shows right away if I get it wrong. I would ask the carpenter to check before we fix it in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to know before paying for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what local employers are hiring for and whether a course is required for those jobs. If nobody can answer, I would keep learning on the site rather than borrow for a guess.

think: I think AI may take my **measurement notes** by 2031.
I cannot call **carpentry safe forever** when robots may reach physical work in 2034.

steps.text: Practise fitting frames and trimming boards with supervision
Wait to decide about a course until local builders explain their hiring needs in 2032

fieldNote: He uses the **extra years** to build specific skills rather than assume protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade is enough time to learn more about what is changing. I would not say it makes construction safe when robots may still reach the site in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI may take the notes and schedules I sometimes help with by 2036, then robots may reach carrying and fitting in 2039. Our children will be older by then and may need different support than they do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep learning practical jobs at the site whenever someone can teach me. In 2037, my partner and I would talk with our older child about study choices when they are closer, because we do not know their future costs now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives us a chance to watch and decide gradually. I still have to pay this month’s mortgage, and I cannot know if my work lasts through the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you steer your children toward a trade now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not choose a path for them before they have made their own interests clear. When the older child chooses subjects, we can sit down and look at the real options together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a ten-year warning give you that a two-year warning does not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could practise several jobs over time and see what builders still need before paying for training. The warning helps me plan, but it cannot cover household bills while I wait.

think: I expect AI could take **notes and schedules** by 2036, then robots may reach physical work in 2039.
**Our children** will be older, with different support needs than they have now.

steps.text: Keep learning practical site jobs through supervised practice
In 2037, discuss the older child’s study choices with partner and child

I would not say **construction is safe** while robots may reach sites in 2039.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it gives me the least time to improve while we have little saved. Paid teaching on site and steady shifts would help more than borrowing for a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I am willing to learn when I can see why a task matters and someone checks my work. A patient carpenter can teach me more than a screen can, and I still have to make the mortgage payment on time.

portrait: Liam is a **43-year-old junior construction worker** living with his partner and two school-age children.
His **thin savings** make cancelled site days more serious than small office changes.
He tries new tools once their usefulness is clear and **someone can guide him**.
He sees the later robot date as a risk, not **permanent protection** for the trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives him little time to improve while the household has little saved.
